notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg0530.tlg043.1st1K-gr: 1.2.1: in the Asclepiades passage the logic is compressed; Asclepiades apparently argued that the heart membranes described by Erasistratus do not exist because Herophilus did not see them. Later in the same section the text reads 'those apparent things that are not apprehended from themselves' (ὅσα οὐκ ἐξ ἑαυτῶν), which contradicts the argument; οὐκ appears to be an error, and 'apprehended from themselves' is translated. The example 'that which one can use well and badly' is quoted elliptically (Stoic: such a thing is not a good). 1.3.1: 'δηλονότι ἀρχὴ τῆς παραδόσεως... ἀπὸ φαινομένων γίνεται' sits awkwardly with the argument and may be corrupt. 'τεχνῶν τεχνῶν' is a dittography and is translated once. 'τὰ τοῦ λαγωοῦ' is taken as the hare's tracks (ἰχνῶν follows). 1.4.1: the quotations about excess, surfeit and evacuation are Hippocratic (Aphorisms). The sentence beginning 'ἐναργοῦς γὰρ ὄντος, ἐφ’ ὧν μὲν...' is corrupt; the translation is tentative.

Line 2: the sentence 'in general, one who judges things joined by connection...' is obscure and probably corrupt; rendered literally. Line 3: the list of common doctrines is loosely punctuated in the edition; 'untested history is not to be accepted' and 'the instruments' are taken as separate items. Line 4: 'οὕτω γὰρ πάντα' is read as 'οὔτε γὰρ πάντα' ('not all'), as the sense requires; the sentence 'οὐδὲν γὰρ, τῶν συμφερόντων...' seems corrupt. In the same line, 'What is a cause is apparent as a cause' contradicts the argument; a negative ('is not apparent as a cause') has probably dropped out. Line 5: 'εἰ τοῦτο ἀδύνατον' ('if this is impossible') seems corrupt, perhaps for 'but this is impossible'. 'ὄπιόν ἐστι κατ’ ἄλληλα' is read as 'ὄπιον κατάλληλον' ('opium is suitable'). 'λιθοτόμῳ' may mean the lithotomist rather than his knife.

In 10.1 the parenthesis 'πᾶσιν γὰρ ὑπερβαίνουσιν ἔνδειξιν' seems corrupt; rendered literally. 'οὔτε γὰρ. τὸ συνεκτικὸν αἴτιον ἐνταῦθά γε δηλοῖ' is garbled: read as δῆλον ('evident'), and a new sentence on henbane seems to begin after 'εὕρηται' without connective; possibly a lacuna. 'αἰτίοιν' read as αἰτίων. 'αἱμόῤῥους' is a snake whose bite was thought to cause bleeding (haemorrhous). In 12.1 'ἀποκτᾶσθαι' is evidently corrupt (sense required: refute/attack); 'τῶν δυναμένων τήρησις κοινή' is obscure, rendered 'observation of the powers'. 'ἀδύνατος ἡ τήρησις' in 12.1 read as 'ἀδύνατον'.

13.1: 'χρόνον δεῖ τηρήσει· παραλαμβάνεσθαι' taken as 'time must be taken into the observation'. 'τὸ βάρος, ὅτι αἰτία ἐστὶ' is elliptical; rendered as heaviness pointing to a cause. 'τίν’ ἂν φήσομεν' read as 'τί ἂν φήσομεν'. 'οὐ γάρ ἐστιν ἄλλα ταῖς συνεκτικαῖς' is obscure, perhaps corrupt; rendering tentative. 'ταῖς ἐπιδρομαῖς' read as 'ταῖς συνδρομαῖς'. 14.1: 'τινὰ κριτὴν εἶχεν καλῶς ἂν περιδέχεσθαι' seems corrupt; rendered by sense as 'accept history without a judge'. 'οὐδὲ ἄχρηστον παραδέχεσθαι' rendered as if 'ἄκριτον' ('uncritically'); the transmitted reading seems faulty. The Homeric quotations are Iliad 9.593, 9.529 and 4.164 / 6.448. Petronas, Apollonius and Dexippus are early physicians.

16.1: 'ἀλλ’ ἐτηρήσατε, φασὶν' ("but you have observed, they say") is awkward in context; the sense requires the Empiricists' reply, and the text may be corrupt (perhaps 'ἀλλ’ ἐρεῖτε' or similar). 17.1: the pepper sentence is elliptical as transmitted. 18.1: 'οὐδὲ παρὰ τὴν διάνοιαν τῆς αἰτίας' is obscure (the negative seems out of place) and is rendered by sense; 'φλεγμονῇ γὰρ τῇ αὐτῇ θεραπείᾳ χρήσεται' may be mispunctuated; 'ἡ γὰρ θεραπεία σύμπτωμά ἐστι' seems corrupt and is rendered by the evident sense ('consists in'). λεπίς taken as copper scale; κήλη as hernia; μελικηρίς as meliceris (honey-like cyst).

In 20.1 'οὐκ ὄντως τυχεῖν δυνατόν' is awkward and may be corrupt; rendered 'it is not really possible for them all to coincide'. In 21.1 'ἔχονται' read as ἔχοντα, and 'τὸ αὐτὸ ἐναντίον' as 'the same thing [does not indicate] contraries' (ἐναντία). In 22.1 'στεγνῶσι δὲ τὸ ἐναντίον' taken as 'on the contrary, constrict'.

Several places look corrupt and are rendered tentatively: 'οὐ γίνονται δὲ, οὐκ ἂν τὰ διαφέροντα πάθη...' (23.1) seems to lack a connective; 'κένωσις... ἐναντία τῷ πάθει' contradicts the argument, and 'not' may have dropped out; 'καὶ ἀνεπιδείκνυται, ὅπερ πάθος ἐστί' is obscure; the sentence beginning 'ἰσχουρίας οὖν οὔσης' needs an implied 'otherwise'. In 25.1 'ὅπερ οὖν παραλαμβάνομεν, ταὐτὸν ἐνδείκνυται πάθος' is unclear, probably 'what we adopt is not what the affection indicates'. The bracketed words in that sentence are conjectural. 'ἀφρόνιτρον' is foam of soda (a form of natron).

Line 26: the sentence 'οὐδὲν τῶν κατὰ φύσιν παρὰ φύσιν φαίνεται, ἀλλ’ ὡς μὲν κατὰ φύσιν, ἢ παρὰ φύσιν φαίνεται' and the following 'οὐχ οἷά ἐστι παρὰ φύσιν, ἀλλ’ ὡς ἔστι' seem corrupt; translated for the evident sense (doctors seek whether a thing is unnatural, not merely what appears). 'ἔπειτα παρὰ φύσιν οὐ φαίνεται' is taken as 'if then the unnatural is not apparent'. Line 28: 'τὴν δὲ χρείαν ἐκ τῶν ἀποτελεσμάτων πολλῶν, καὶ τούτων ἐξ ἑαυτῶν, μὴ καταλαμβανομένης τῆς ῥύσεως γιγνωσκομένης' is garbled; rendered by likely sense. 'τὴν χαλεπωτάτην τῆς κρίσεως' taken as 'the very great difficulty of the judgement'. 'κατὰ τὸ ἄδηλον διαφορουμένων' refers to patients losing substance through imperceptible transpiration.

32.1: 'διαφέροντα φανερά' is read as a slip for 'συμφέροντα φανερά' (evident beneficial things). The sentence 'καὶ εἰ ἄρα νοσημάτων ... ἐνεδείκνυντο ἂν τὸ συμφέρον' seems corrupt; the translation is literal and the sense uncertain. 'οὐδενός τινος ὑπ’ αὐτῆς ἀναιρεθέντος' is obscure; it may mean 'although nothing had been done for them'. 'τόπῳ, καιρῷ' in the surgical koinotētes: other sources give 'by place, by magnitude'. 33.1: the singular 'αὐτῷ' (him) has no clear antecedent; perhaps Thessalus is meant, or the text should read 'αὐτοῖς'. 34.1: 'εἰ ἡ κοινότης ἐπιδείκνυσι, καὶ ὃ ἐνδείκνυται, οὐκ ἐπὶ μέρους ἀδιαφορεῖν δεῖ' is obscure, and the rendering is tentative.

καιρός is rendered 'time(s)' throughout this discussion of the times of diseases and remedies, following the earlier lines, rather than the glossary's 'right moment'. ἄνεσις is rendered 'abatement'. In 38.1 the phrase ποίων ἄν τις ὑπαγόρευσιν διάστημα φαίη seems corrupt, and the sense 'what interval one could name as prescribing [it]' is a guess. The clause μήποτε οὖν σκοποὶ ὑποστάσει οὐ διαφέρουσι also seems corrupt or misplaced, and is translated literally.

In 43.1 the argument about ἐπίτασις ('intensification', apparently meaning convalescent recovery) seems confused or corrupt; translated as it stands. ἀλφοί and λεῦκαι are white skin conditions (alphos, leuke). In 42.1 'καὶ ἡ σύμμετρος' is obscure; taken as 'a moderate [power]'. In 45.1 'καιρὸς δὲ τροφῆς ἢ ποσότητος' is rendered as written; ποιότητος ('quality') may be intended.

47.1: the sentence 'δι’ ὧν δὲ χρὴ κωλύειν τὴν ἐπὶ μέρους, ὧν τὸ κωλύειν αὔξεσθαι ἐνδείκνυται, ἢ τὸ δι’ ὧν...' seems corrupt; the rendering gives the probable sense (the Rationalist reply that the beginning, too, does not indicate the means). 'μὴ τῇ ἀρχῇ, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῇ διαθέσει' presumably lacks μόνον; translated as 'not [only]'. 'μίαν ἐπιπλοκὴν ... τὴν τῶν παθῶν' is obscure; rendered as referring to the Methodists' 'mixed' class as one kind among the affections. 49.1: 'ταῦτα δὲ κατ’ αὐτούς· ἢν τὰ στέλλοντα αἱ ἀρχαὶ τῶν νοσημάτων' is corrupt (ἢν perhaps for εἰ, with a verb such as ἐνδείκνυνται lost); translated by conjecture. 'ἑκατέρας' probably stands for ἑκάστης.

nodes.text: GALEN TO THRASYBULUS ON THE BEST SECT.

Every medical theorem, and indeed every theorem in general, must first be true, then useful, then consistent with the principles laid down. For it is by these three that a sound theorem is judged, so that, if any of the things mentioned is lacking in a theorem, one should not call it a theorem at all. For since the arts consist of theorems, and not of any chance theorems, but [their] apprehensions must first form a system, and then also contribute to something useful, it is therefore necessary that every theorem be true, and useful, and have a certain consistency, not only with the principles laid down, but also with the remaining theorems. For in so far as every theorem falls under apprehension, it must be true, since there are no apprehensions of false things. And in so far as it tends towards some end that bears on life, each of the theorems must be useful and necessary. And the system of apprehensions must be sought in the agreement of the theorems with one another and with the principle laid down. And since, just as the system of those who are ruled is conceived as under one ruler, so too the theorem is referred to the principle laid down. For this reason every theorem must be true and useful and consistent. And if every theorem of an art is judged by these three, it is clear that medical theorems too would be judged by these same [three]. Since, then, it is not always evident what sort of thing the true is and how it might be judged, and neither the useful nor the consistent is easy to apprehend, one must before all else set out certain marks and criteria of these.

The true, then, is judged by the agreement of the statement with the underlying things. But since of the underlying things some are apparent and others hidden, and of the apparent ones some are apprehensible from themselves, such as white and black, while others are apprehensible not from themselves but from other things, such as what is apprehended through signs; and again, of the hidden ones some are evident and are called so, such as 'twice two is four', while others are apprehended through demonstration, such as 'that which one can use well and badly', and what follows; one must always refer the statement and the theorem to the kind of the underlying thing which the statement is about, or with regard to which the theorem was made. And if it is about one of the apparent things, [one must] fit it to that; but if about one of the hidden things, one must consider whether it agrees with one of the hidden things. The ways of judging apparent and hidden things differ. For those apparent things that are apprehensible from themselves are judged by sense, such as white and black. Hence one must laugh at those physicians who try to make the judgement of apparent things not by the sense organs but by some demonstration; as, for example, Asclepiades, discussing the membranes that grow on the heart, says that Erasistratus has gone astray; for Herophilus, who had dissected much, had not seen [them]; whereas he could have gone, as was proper, to the examination of the apparent things and pronounced on the matter, and not put his trust in foolish opinions. So of the apparent things that are apprehended from themselves, the criteria, as I said, are the sense organs. But of things that are apparent, yet apprehended not from themselves but from other things, the criterion is joint observation; I mean of things apprehended through signs. Again, of hidden things, just as the differences are several, so the criteria too differ. Among hidden things some are evident, such as that it is impossible for the same man to be at once both in Athens and in Egypt, while others are apprehended through demonstration. The test of evident things is the common notion of all men; the test of things apprehended through demonstration is agreement with what is agreed. The test of what is agreed in turn divides into several. For what is agreed is judged either by [agreement] with apparent things, or with evident things, or with things demonstrated. How, then, one must judge the true, and what contributes to the judgement of the true, has been stated.

Next we must speak of the useful theorem. The useful theorem, then, is judged by reference to the end of the art. It must first of all be apprehensible. For if it is impossible, like 'the bile of the hippocentaur cures apoplexy', because it is unapprehensible, it becomes useless for that reason. Next, its apprehension must not be shared with laymen, but peculiar to practitioners of the art. It is for this reason, indeed, that we say those are mistaken who think that apparent things are the principle of the art. For neither is the art composed of apparent things, nor is the teaching of the art derived from apparent things. For no one teaches the apparent things, but the theorems based on the apparent things, which are not apparent. These, then, one might reasonably call the principle of the art too; I mean the theorems based on apparent things, since clearly the principle of the teaching of the art comes from apparent things. For if someone were to say that the apparent things are the principle of the art, he will fail to notice that he thinks art no different from lack of art. For since the apprehension of apparent things is alike for the practitioner and the layman, it is clear that in this respect the practitioner will have no advantage over the layman, nor indeed will he have an art, if the apprehension of the same things is also the same for practitioner and layman. Apparent things, then, could rightly be called the principle of the discovery of theorems; but apparent things are not the principle of the art. For just as one might reasonably call the [tracks] of the hare the principle of finding the hare, but no one with any sense would call [them] the principle of the hare, since the hare is not composed of its tracks, so too [one might call] apparent things the principle of the discovery of theorems. One might rightly say that, starting from these, those who constituted it constituted [the art], but no longer [that they are the principle] of the art. For one must refer principles to the quality of that of which they are the principles. And so the principles of the art too should not be manifest to laymen, for not all the arts are evident to them either; and further, the principles of the arts are taught, whereas apparent things are not taught. Therefore one could not reasonably call apparent things the principle of the art.

For theorems are constituted either on the basis of apparent things, or of things apprehended from other things, or of things previously demonstrated, or of evident things, in some such way as this. On the basis of apparent things thus: someone, having come across several people wounded in the heart who died, sought the cause of the death. Reasoning, then, he found that they died neither through lack of strength nor through want of material for remedies, but because of the vital function of the part. Recognising, then, that without the activity of this part and the function that accrues from it to the body the animal cannot survive, and combining by reasoning what had been found in the apparent things, he made this theorem: if someone is wounded in the heart, he will die. What has been found by reasoning in consequence of apparent things, and stated universally, is a theorem. Rather, the theorem is constituted on apparent things as [it is] from the apparent things in inflammation: if someone has inflammation, he has a resistant swelling which brings throbbing pain. Apparent things, then, become the principle of the discovery of theorems, while theorems found consequentially on apparent things are the principle of the constitution of an art. And on the basis of apparent things the theorem is constituted in some such way. On the basis of things apprehended from other things the theorem is constituted thus: if someone has these symptoms, he is in a plethora of blood; he who has these accompanying [signs] has suffered [an affection of] the liver, or kidney, or some such thing. On the basis of things previously demonstrated the theorem is constituted thus. When it has been demonstrated that digestion exists, and that what is digested is dissolved and moistened and then in this way distributed, and that the sick need foods which do not require much working up, on this basis this theorem arises: 'moist regimens all benefit those in fever'. On the basis of evident things thus: 'and everything excessive is hostile to nature', and 'neither surfeit nor hunger nor anything else is good which goes beyond nature'. And 'where surfeit breeds diseases, evacuation cures'. For since it is evident, in some cases, that [these belong] among things beyond [our] strength, and in others that, when the producing cause is removed, what comes about would not come about, the theorems stated were composed. Every theorem is universal and certain. Those, then, are mistaken who say the art is conjectural because it has conjectural theorems. For it is not called conjectural on account of the theorem, since these are fixed, but on account of the practice and the activity of those who treat. For this, having uncertain success, makes the art conjectural, since the theorems of all the arts are alike certain and fixed. But because the successes of all the arts are not certain, some of the arts are said to be conjectural, namely those which, as I said, have uncertain success. And since we said that the useful must be judged by reference to the end, it would be necessary to point out the end of the art, so that, this having been made evident, it may be evident to what one must refer in judging the useful.

Of the arts, then, some produce things that do not exist, as shipbuilding does; some preserve things that have come into being, as navigation does; and some do both, as housebuilding does. In the arts that either produce or preserve there is one way of success, and so the judgement of the useful is simple. In those that both produce and preserve it is not easy. For one must not think useless what does not contribute to preservation, but must inquire whether it contributes something to producing what does not exist. Medicine, then, is one of the arts that produce and preserve. Yet one should not suppose that the end of the art is double, namely to produce what does not exist, such as health, and to safeguard it when it is present. For, they say, since it produces health and preserves it through the same words, it would have a double end. Now if the same theorems did not plainly lead to both ends, then, since the ends differ, the arts too would differ, and there would be two medicines. But since the theorems are the same while the aims differ, it would be one art having different aims. They do not know that the aim of the art is one, health, and the end is one, to attain health, while the ways of success differ. So the aim does not change, nor does the end, according to the way of [attaining] health. For since we have knowledge of the things that naturally do harm, in some cases we secure health by removing the harmful things, and in others we preserve it by avoiding them. So in medicine one must judge the useful by considering sometimes whether it contributes to producing health, and sometimes whether it contributes to preserving it.

Some think that what is consistent is judged by coexistence. They do not know that many things coexist with one another, yet no consistency is seen in them; just as we say that it being day coexists with breathing, yet there is no consistency [of the one] with it. So consistency must not be judged by coexistence. Rather, where something is necessarily abolished along with a thing when that thing is abolished, and is posited when it is posited, that must be held to be consistent with it. And in general, one who judges things joined by connection must judge [them] by a test, in those cases where one needs to make a consistent test. For the test of some arguments, then, the consistency sought is necessary. Whether it also contributes to the judgement of medical theorems, one might perhaps inquire. For it is not enough to recognise whether a theorem that is useful and true is a medical one; one must nonetheless always hold to what is consistent.

Since, then, every argument and every theorem is judged by these three, and there are three sects in medicine, that of the Rationalists, that of the Empiricists and that of the Methodists, come, let us use these criteria to examine the sects too, so that we may attach ourselves to the sound one. It is necessary first to set out what the sects have in common, and what is peculiar to each of them, and then, in this way, to make the test of them in order. These, then, are common to the three sects: that the apparent theorems are useful; analogical reasoning, observation, history, transition to the similar; that untested history is not to be accepted; the instruments; the manner of applying remedies; that some things are apprehended from others; that in the same circumstances the same things must be done; that health is maintained and diseases are treated by additions and subtractions; that one must avoid the use of harmful things, both for maintaining health and for getting rid of diseases; that trial is possible and useful for apprehending the material applied. For nourishing and non-nourishing, purgative and destructive things have been apprehended by trial.

The Empiricists have stopped at this common [ground], saying that not only the powers but also the beneficial things have been found by trial. The Methodists, on the common ground already stated, say something different from the Empiricists. For they say that apart from learning the powers of the things administered, nothing else useful results from trial. For none of the beneficial things themselves can be taken simply from observation, the beneficial things [being taken] from certain apparent things that have been observed. The Rationalists have taken a middle position between these. For they say that not all beneficial things are taken from observation, as the Empiricists say, nor yet are [all] found from indication, as the Methodists think, but that some are found from observation, such as deadly and venomous things, and others from indication, in cases where the causes are found. The Methodists, then, agree with the Rationalists in so far as they think that the beneficial is taken from indication; but in that [they take it] from different things, they disagree. For the Methodists think that beneficial things are taken as indicated by certain apparent things; the Rationalists, by no means from apparent things, but from hidden ones. For since they hold that indications come from causes, and causes, as causes, are not apparent, it is clear that for them indications could not come from apparent things; and they say that apparent things guide [us] towards the apprehension of things able to indicate. On this point, then, the Empiricists in turn agree with the Rationalists, saying that indication of the beneficial comes from nothing apparent. Another point is common and agreed by all physicians, that apparent things are serviceable. The Empiricists say that apparent things are serviceable for observing what goes with apparent things, because there is observation upon some of them, and because from them one can apprehend the things able to indicate. The Methodists say that apparent things are serviceable as being beneficial. Here again it is common to Empiricists and Methodists that what is not hidden is apprehended from apparent things, [that] from which the indication of beneficial things comes. Common to the Empiricists and the Rationalists is observing beneficial things upon apparent things. Common to the Rationalists and the Methodists is that useful things are apprehended upon apparent things. The Methodists say that the beneficial itself is apprehended from apparent things, while the Rationalists say that the things able to indicate the beneficial are found from apparent things, but nothing beneficial [is]. To those who think that something beneficial is found from evident causes, as in the case of a splinter, it must be said that in these cases the beneficial is found not as from apparent things but as from causes. But the cause, as a cause, is not apparent, but is apprehended from the symptoms. At any rate, if a grain of sand or a little splinter lying on the surface causes no pain and does not bring us to perception [of it], we do not apprehend it. For whatever produces [something] is not [thereby] the cause of something. What is a cause is apparent as a cause. For things that are in some relation to something are not apparent in respect of their being in relation to something; the relative things themselves are apparent, for instance father, slave, brother and the like: each of these is itself apparent, but their relations to other things are not apparent.

Since, then, we have handed down the criteria of arguments and have gone through what is common to and peculiar to the sects, it would next be necessary to make the test of each of the sects, and then in this way to attach ourselves to the sound opinion. The Empiricists and the Methodists, arguing against the Rationalists, say that the apprehension of hidden things is useless, for nothing useful is found from hidden things. To this the Rationalists reply to each sect separately. And first they say to the Empiricists that apparent things do not suffice for observing beneficial things upon them; for there is need of hidden things too, since it is from these that the indications of beneficial things come. A proof: (you yourselves do not observe upon all apparent things, but upon some) that the apparent things upon which one must observe have something more, which is not apparent. If so, hidden things would be serviceable. So apparent things are either taken as apparent for the discovery of beneficial things, and all will be useful, or not. Now to say that all are useful is implausible. But if not all are useful, the useful ones must have something more than being apparent, which it belongs not to perception to apprehend but to reason. And hidden things are apprehended by reason; so reason is useful, and so are hidden things. For if apparent things, in so far as they are apparent, plainly do not differ from one another, then all alike serve for observation, even upon themselves, so that there would be [observation] even upon the smallest things, both past and present, if this is impossible. For how could there be any observation upon the bedding, and the bed on which the patient lay, and the like? It is clear, then, that observation does not take place upon apparent things as they are apparent, for then it would take place upon all alike, but upon something else, which is not apparent. If so, hidden things would be useful. But further, they say, from where is it apprehended that upon these particular apparent things it is possible to observe, but upon those no longer? For it is not easy to know this from the apparent things themselves, in so far as they are apparent. For then everyone, even laymen, would know upon which apparent things observation must be made, and your experience would not differ at all from the inexperience of laymen. But if it does not strike everyone upon which apparent things observations must be made, and this is apprehensible only to practitioners, then beneficial things are observed upon apparent things not as they are apparent. For [the fact] that this apparent thing is one upon which there can be observation, and that one is not, is no longer apparent, but is hidden. And it is very useful to know this; therefore hidden things are useful. In addition to what has been said, since the Empiricists say that observations must be made upon these particular antecedents and these particular present things (for this is indeed why they inquire into the past), and the present things too are infinite, and it is not possible to observe upon infinite things, plainly such observation would be impossible. To the Methodists, who think that apparent things are indicative of beneficial things, the Rationalists say this. Apparent things are apprehensible from themselves, and so will be apparent to laymen too. And since the koinotētes [communities] also indicate, and what is taken from them strikes [us] together with the things indicating, plainly the koinotētes will give indications to laymen, and you will differ in nothing from laymen. That the indication of beneficial things does not come from the affections can be shown by these [arguments]. When the same affection, such as inflammation, is present in different places, such as the eyes, or the liver, or the stomach, they need not the same treatment but different ones. For to an inflamed eye opium is suitable, but to the stomach and liver something else. And oil is harmful to the eye, but soothes the other parts when inflamed. It is clear, then, that beneficial things are not taken from the affections. For the same remedy would have been adopted in all cases, the affection being the same, if the affection were indicative of beneficial things. The Methodist's view can also be refuted thus: when the same affection is in the same place, people need different treatment according to the difference of the cause, as in retention of urine. For if it is a stone, we use a lithotomy knife; if an excess of urine, a catheter; if inflammation, a poultice. But if the indications of beneficial things came from the affections, then with one underlying affection one and the same treatment would be adopted. But one treatment is not adopted when the same affection underlies; therefore the indications of beneficial things do not come from the affections.

Now that these things have been set out in summary, it would be useful to sketch what indication is, and how the useful is apprehended from indication; what observation is, and how useful things are observed through observation; and what analogical reasoning is, and how the useful is apprehended from it. Just as, then, among apparent things some are apprehensible of themselves, for instance white and black, while others are apprehended by joint observation, as things known through signs, so too beneficial things are apprehended by indication. For the beneficial things present themselves together with the things that indicate [them], and there is no need of any reasoning. It is for this reason, indeed, that even irrational animals withdraw from burning heat and cold and, in short, from all things whose nature is to harm, evidently because the beneficial presents itself together [with them]. And in the case of a splinter stuck fast, or of anything else, no one makes the choice by reasoning. What happens, then, with things assented to because they are evident (for in all [such] cases, which go beyond indication, our mind assents to what is evident), this also happens with things apprehended from indication. So a certain analogy is preserved between indication and apparent and evident things. For when the beneficial coincides with the harmful things, then we use neither observation nor reasoning: the harmful things themselves indicate the beneficial. Observation, on the other hand, bears a certain analogy to the things apprehended through signs. For just as there we say [things] are apprehended by joint observation, so here too observation of the beneficial comes about. For observation of the beneficial comes about in cases that have very often turned out in the same way, without apprehension of the causes that produce [them], as with purslane for teeth set on edge. For neither [is] the containing cause evident here, nor has the beneficial been found by any reasoning. In the case of those who have taken henbane, or have consumed some other such poison, the treatment is at first adopted from both the cause and the place, but later, for lack of [knowledge of] the cause, we then use what has been observed. For at the beginning we adopt vomiting, the cause indicating the choice of it, and the place supplying the manner of the choice. But later, being ignorant of the cause, we use what has been observed, wine and milk. The useful is apprehended by analogical reasoning when the cause is unknown and there is no observation, but there is something most similar [to go on] from the symptoms. For in such cases the useful cannot be taken from indication, since the cause is unknown; and since no observation has been made, we are compelled, attending to the similarity of the symptoms, to make the transition to the similar. For when someone has been bitten by a haemorrhous and then bleeds, not knowing the cause by which he suffers this, nor having observed [it], we use the things that work against haemorrhages from a wound. On some such reasoning the Cnidian physicians tried to treat those who have pus in the lung, using the transition to the similar. For since everything present in the lung is brought up by coughing, they drew out the tongue and introduced into the windpipe some liquid able to provoke a violent cough, so that through the similarity of the symptom the pus might be brought up. Analogical reasoning, then, comes about upon the transition to the similar: for in reasoning analogically we pass from similar things to similar things. The Empiricists, however, have used the transition to the similar differently, and not as we do. For they say that the transition to the similar takes place from remedies to remedies, or from affections to affections. From remedies to remedies, thus: when the same symptoms attend the things adopted, then we make the transition to the similar, as from apple to medlar. But it must be said to them that such a transition to the similar is impossible for you. For do you pass from the similar to the similar using reasoning, or observation? If by observation, what takes place and is known is observation, and not transition to the similar. But if by reasoning, they must be asked whether they pass from the similar to the similar attending to the similarity of all the symptoms, or of some. If, then, they say of all, nothing will be found similar to anything in all respects. For things that differ from one another in nothing whatever are the same, and not similar. But if they say they are content with the similarity of some symptoms, we shall say: do you attend to similarities of shape or colour, or to those of hardness or softness, or rather do you judge the similarity by those of taste, or by something of that kind? And if they say by taste, or by anything else whatever, they will plainly concede that they apprehend beneficial things in respect of that by which they benefit. From which it is clear that they will also be compelled to concede that they know harmful things in respect of that by which they harm. For beneficial things benefit by their contrariety to harmful things. If, then, the medlar is chosen for dysenteric patients because it has a quality of taste resembling the apple, one must know that it benefits by its quality in respect of taste. And since this is plainly astringent, there presents itself together with this apprehension [the fact] that harmful things are of the contrary quality or power. But if remedies are opposed to an apprehensible cause, it is clear that hidden things are apprehensible, and useful to be known.

How, then, the useful is apprehended from indication has been stated. Now we shall set out the outline definitions of each of them. Indication, then, is the apprehension of what benefits that presents itself together with the apprehension of what harms, without observation or reasoning. Trial is the apprehension and memory of what has been seen very often or in the same way. Or thus: indication is when the beneficial presents itself together with things being apprehended, without demonstration and observation. Trial is the observation and memory of what has been seen very often and in the same way. Observation is the same thing as trial. Analogical reasoning is the comparison and apprehension of beneficial causes by similarities. Next, then, having set out what is peculiar to each sect, we shall make our rebuttal of each of them, I mean of the Empiricists and the Methodists. These are peculiar to the Empiricists: the observation of beneficial things upon syndromes, history, and the transition to the similar as they hold it takes place. For the Rationalists use the transition to the similar in another way, as we shall show the difference as we proceed.

Whoever argues against the Empiricists must attack the observation upon syndromes in two ways. For observation of the powers is common [to all], but that upon symptoms is peculiar to them. For one must either do away with it altogether as impossible, or grant that it is possible, but show that without reason it is impossible. First, then, that observation is impossible without reason, one might show by the following. The Empiricists concede that they do not make their observation upon all apparent symptoms. For they say they do not observe upon, say, fairness or whiteness, or a snub or a hooked nose. And yet they do observe a certain difference in colours, as with jaundiced patients, and in shape, as with fractures and dislocations. But not, at any rate, in the cases mentioned before. For just as, they say, those who claim to take beneficial things from indication do not say that all things indicate (for the Methodists say that some of the apparent things indicate, and not all, and the Rationalists [some] of the hidden things, and not all), so too the Empiricists say they make observation not upon all symptoms but upon some. For they do not think that all past things, nor all present ones, are useful for observation. For instance, someone has been bitten by a rabid dog; the Empiricist, coming in, inquires only whether [it was] by a rabid one, and of the other antecedent things he examines not a single one; and likewise with present things: for [he observes] neither upon straightness of hair, as I said, nor upon curliness. It is right, then, to ask them the reason why they observe beneficial things not upon all symptoms but upon some, when the symptoms do not differ at all, insofar as they are apparent, both those upon which observation takes place and the others that are useless. Let them say, then, what it is that indicates which of the symptoms are useful: is it apparent, or hidden? If they say it is apparent, that by which the useful symptoms are distinguished, and upon which observation must take place, we shall say again that this, being apparent, differs in no way, insofar as it is apparent, from the useless symptoms. But if, again, one should say that what indicates the useful symptoms is hidden, they will concede that hidden things are useful for the observation of symptoms. But hidden things are apprehensible by nothing other than reason. So, if [the knowledge] of hidden things is useful for observation upon syndromes, and these are apprehended by nothing but reason, it is clear that observation without reason is impossible. By this argument, then, [one can] compel them to concede that reason is useful for observation. They, however, replying to us, say that they have apprehended by trial which of the symptoms are useful too; and that they have observed this too, that upon these symptoms one must observe, but upon those no longer. To this the answer is short. For since the symptoms upon which one must not observe are infinite, it would have been impossible to have observed upon all of them this very thing, that one must not observe upon them; for it is impossible to observe upon infinitely many. Finally, then, driven in from every side, it remains for them to say that it has come about by chance that they observe upon these symptoms and no longer upon those; and what could be more ridiculous than that? This argument, then, ends here.

That observation upon syndromes is impossible, I shall show by the following. The Empiricists say, then, that observation takes place not upon one case, nor upon two, but upon very many [cases] that have been seen very often and that are in the same condition. If, then, we ask them whether they observe the beneficial things upon the same kinds of symptoms, they will necessarily say that they observe upon the same kinds. For if in one case there is, say, fever and inflammation, but in another an excretion of bile by vomiting or through the anus occurs, it is not possible to make the same observation. They will by no means say, then, that it is enough for the symptoms to be the same in kind; they must also be equal in number. For if the same symptoms remain, but not all of them, or more of them, the syndrome is altered, and there is need of another observation. For observation must take place upon the same kinds and the same numbers. How the whole treatment is altered by an excess or a deficiency of symptoms must be considered from this. There is, then, a treatment that has been observed for inflammation. If, then, one removes one symptom of the inflammation, such as sensation, the treatment is altered too. For instead of an inflammation there is an induration, and the same treatment is not suitable. In this way, then, the treatment is altered by a deficiency of a symptom. By excess, in this way: if fever or syncope is added to the inflammation, then with the excess of symptoms the syndrome becomes different, and a different treatment is also adopted. And the symptoms must not only be the same in kind and equal in number, but they must also neither exceed nor fall short in magnitude. For the treatment is altered according to the magnitudes of the symptoms too. For we do not stitch superficial cuts, nor would anyone use fasting [for them]. But when a large cut has occurred, we adopt fasting, and phlebotomy, and wound clamps, and the like. And it is not enough for the symptoms to be the same in kind, and equal in number, and similar in magnitude; time too must be taken into the observation. For some remedies are adopted when diseases are beginning, and others when they are at their peak. 'For when diseases are beginning, if anything seems [needful] to be set in motion, set it in motion; but when they are at their peak, keep quiet,' said Hippocrates. And when an inflammation is beginning we use repellents, but after this poultices and things able to disperse what has flowed in. One must also observe the order together with the things mentioned, for the syndrome is altered by the order too. Because of this the treatment must also be altered. For we treat those who have gone mad and then had fever in one way, and those who have had fever and then gone mad in another. For affections become fatal or not fatal according to the order of the symptoms, as is clear from the outcomes. Fever after a convulsion is not only without danger, but even resolves the disease; but a convulsion after fever is fatal. And since the syndrome is altered by the order of the symptoms, as is clear from the outcomes, it is necessary to concede that the treatment differs too. Since, then, the symptoms must not only be the same in kind, and equal in number, and similar in magnitude, but the same time and the same order must also be preserved, if the observation is to be sound, and since it is impossible in the whole of life for all the things mentioned to befall alike, I will not say several, but even two sick people, it is clear that observation upon the syndrome will be impossible. That it is impossible to grant all the things mentioned in all or in several [cases], one might show by the following. Affections become different according to the cause, and the affected places, and the ages, and according to habits, and according to the magnitudes of the symptoms, and according to natures, and according to seasons and regions; it is altogether impossible to grant of two people that they are alike in every respect. Therefore observation upon syndromes is impossible. And even if two [cases] should be found without variation, not even so is observation possible, because it must take place upon more [cases]. 'But how,' they say, 'do you establish your own doctrine?' For we seem to them to be unable to observe both upon symptoms and upon powers. For that hellebore purges, and the [remedies] for venomous creatures, have been apprehended by observation. And in the case of teeth set on edge, the cause has certainly not been apprehended, but that purslane relieves it has been observed. We must say to them, then, that we, delimiting which of the symptoms are useful by their reference to the targets, judge what is useful also by its use. Having apprehended, then, all the symptoms brought on by causes, such as heaviness, and those from places, such as difficulty in breathing, and those from the power, such as fainting, we find that these are useful, and the rest useless. Since, then, we have circumscribed the useful symptoms by their reference to the targets, we consider useful those that are symptoms of a cause, or of a place, or of the power, and useless those that are not. And so, even if we do not apprehend either the causes producing disease or the affected places, by having, as I said, a power of discriminating between useful and useless symptoms, even if we cannot make our observations upon the things that produced [the disease], as upon causes or affected places, as when blood is troublesome and we have not apprehended that it is blood that is producing the disease, yet setting out from the heaviness, the symptom brought on, [and knowing] that the heaviness [points to] a cause, we can observe upon them. So too with difficulty in breathing: not knowing whether it is a symptom of the stomach, or the lung, or the liver, or the diaphragm, or some other place being affected, but knowing only that it is [of] a place, we can observe upon them, as if upon the place itself. But those that are symptoms neither of a place, nor of a cause, nor of the power, we reject as superfluous. We must speak, then, to the Empiricists about the usefulness and uselessness [of symptoms], according to the targets upon which we observe: [namely] that we observe upon the kinds of symptoms alone [in cases] where there is no need of power, or of right moment, or of magnitude, or of order, or of anything else, as [we observe] purslane upon teeth set on edge. 'What then prevents us too,' they will perhaps say, 'from observing in this way?' If [you do so] in those cases, we shall say, in which a kind of symptoms is observed, as we too [said] before, then in the remaining cases, in which there is need of right moment and magnitude and power, you no longer agree with us. But if they say, 'Several symptoms follow upon the bite of a haemorrhous, and you have observed nothing upon these,' what shall we say? That we observe not upon the symptoms, but upon the antecedent cause; and we seek out the symptoms for the apprehension of the antecedent causes upon which we have observed. For when we do not know the cause, and are at a loss for treatment by indication, we adopt observation upon the antecedent causes. And we observe not only upon causes, but also upon a single place. So upon an affection of the liver and upon an affection of the spleen we have observed certain things. And if they say that one symptom follows each of these, we shall say: sometimes not one, but many. And we busy ourselves with the many, not in order to observe upon them, but in order to apprehend that upon which we observe: [namely,] in the case of liver patients, that the liver is affected, upon which the observation takes place, and likewise in other cases. For the most part, however, observation takes place upon the antecedent cause. For purslane has not been observed upon teeth set on edge [as such], but upon the condition produced by sour or harsh things. At any rate, purslane does no good to those whose teeth are set on edge from a flux, or through vomiting, or from people sawing. So having first sought out the cause from which the teeth-setting-on-edge has arisen, we then use it accordingly. And the things adopted in such cases are not opposed to the antecedent causes. For they are not other than [those opposed] to the containing [causes]. These things, then, might reasonably be said regarding having observation upon syndromes. One must further ask the Empiricist how the right moments for applying remedies are observed, or the measures of the remedies, or the right moments for food, or its quantity.

That the history they speak of is both useless and impossible, I shall now show. The Empiricists make use of history for some such reason as this. Often certain diseases occur for which no remedy has been observed by them. So that they might have some resource in this case too, and not wait upon what happens of itself, they make use of history; and not for this reason only, but for the sake of concise teaching. For it is impossible for the learner to meet with all the symptoms and to make the observation upon them himself. So that one may not be learning forever, but may at some time also practise the art, for this reason they say that history is useful for healing. History is either of present things, as in 'They kill the men, and the great fire levels [the city]', or of things that happened before, as in 'The Curetes were fighting, and the Aetolians steadfast in battle.' But never of future things. For 'There will be a day when sacred Ilium shall perish' is not history, but rather prognosis. The Empiricists for the most part use history of things that happened before. For they say that history is the narration of things tried often in the same way. We must say to them that, if they say that all the things recorded are true, [then] someone would do well to accept history without a judge. But since that is not so, some criterion of history must be found, by which we shall distinguish the truth from falsehoods. For indeed physicians not only do not agree about the same thing, but even hold contrary opinions. For some led those with fever through starvation, and did not even give them water, while others gave barley gruel from the start; and others took care that the patient should never swallow barley. Petronas gave even roast pork and rather undiluted dark wine, made [them] vomit, and gave cold water to drink, as much as they wanted. But Apollonius and Dexippus, the hearers of Hippocrates, gave not only no wine but not even water; having made wax ladles, of which there were twelve to the sixth part of a kotylē, they measured out two or three of these ladles to the patients. Since there is so great a contrariety, then, how should a criterion of history not have been provided? Having compelled them, then, to concede that history should not be accepted uncritically (for in this way we shall show that history is useless), we shall ask whether they judge history by reason or by trial. But by reason they cannot. For they reject it; and besides, each thing is judged by that by which it is apprehended. They say that beneficial things have been apprehended by trial; by trial, then, they must also be judged. For as it is with other things, so here too: someone recorded that snow cools. If the history is to be judged, one must use the same criterion by which the recorder apprehended [it]. The Rationalist, then, will be able to judge history from the cause. For when someone has recorded that, in a man who had his vessels distended and weighed down, a haemorrhage occurring put an end to the discomfort and the heaviness, he tests whether this is true by looking to the cause that brings on the symptoms, and considering whether the haemorrhage could be opposed to the cause. And finding that the heaviness and the distension arise from plethora, while haemorrhage diminishes plethora, he has apprehended that the history is true, and he needs nothing else for the test. But where we do not apprehend the cause, trial itself judges the history. For if someone appears to report to him that purslane relieved teeth set on edge, he will use trial for the judgement. In this way, then, the Empiricist too must make the judgement of history by trial. But if trial judges history, history becomes superfluous and useless. But some of the Empiricists say: 'We judge history by attending to the trustworthiness of those who record it.' And when we ask, 'How do you judge trustworthiness, since different people err and succeed in different things?', they say: 'When the recorder does not record out of some love of reputation, nor out of partisan attachment to doctrines, nor out of some contentiousness, then we say that what is recorded is true.' To this we must say, first: [what if] the recorder records for none of the reasons mentioned, but because he has been deceived? Is what has been recorded true, then, because it is recorded neither for reputation, nor out of partisan attachment to doctrines, nor out of some contentiousness? Secondly, when they require the recorder to be a wise physician, they abandon judging the history and judge a wise man; and such judgement belongs to philosophers and physicians. And from what source is it even possible to judge that what is recorded is recorded neither for reputation, nor out of doctrines with partisanship, nor out of contentiousness? In addition to what has been said, for the judgement of trustworthiness they also use a criterion rejected by themselves; for in saying 'when it is recorded neither for reputation nor out of contentiousness', they set out causes on account of which one must trust the recorder. So that, if for nothing else, at least for this the causes that are sought are useful. And we do nothing more, but say that one must busy oneself with the 'why', which they too are evidently doing in their judgement of history. But we use the 'why', and in general the cause, for judging the matter stated, while the Empiricists [use it] for testing the character of the recorder. And judging characters is the proper business not of physicians but of philosophers. The Empiricists also say this, to the effect that one need not judge history by trial. For they say: 'Just as you, because some people record that Crete is an island, have apprehended that there is an island Crete, although you have not been eyewitnesses of Crete, so we too, when many agree about the same things, do not need to judge history by trial, but have trusted the opinion of the many.' But we, we shall say, have trusted about Crete that it exists, setting out at least from these reasonable grounds: that someone sails from there to here, and again from here to there, and that certain Cretans are friends of ours here, or again [there are those] to whom we send letters and from whom letters are brought to us. And further, that all men agree about it, even the most hostile. But about matters of medicine they agree about almost nothing, and that though physicians are few in comparison with all mankind; and they not only do not agree, but even hold the most contrary opinions, as we showed a little earlier. For these reasons, then, there is need of some criterion for testing history in medicine. And since the Empiricists also say that of things apprehended, some are apprehended by sense, such as redness, and others by way of recollection, such as things apprehended through certain signs, but nothing is apprehended by way of indication, nor in the other mode rejected by them; and yet they apprehend that Crete is an island: it is clear that either they have not apprehended that Crete was an island, or, if they have apprehended it, there is some third mode of apprehension. These things, then, have been said to establish that the history they babble about is superfluous.

That it is also impossible to have apprehension of something beneficial from history, one could establish briefly. For since observation must take place, as we showed earlier, not only upon the kind and number of symptoms, but also upon their magnitude and right moment, and these cannot be recorded without the targets, it is clear that history too would be impossible. That treatments also differ according to magnitudes, right moments and order has been shown. Moreover, from the arguments by which we established that it is impossible to make an observation upon a syndrome, it is possible to establish from the same arguments that it is not possible to make a history either. For surely, if it is not possible to make an observation, it is not possible to record things that have not been observed.

Next we must speak about transition to the similar. The Empiricists needed transition to the similar for the following reasons. Since the things upon which observations had to be made were very many and almost infinite, and the beneficial things were infinite too, and it was impossible for anyone to observe in person upon all or most of them, for this reason they needed both history and transition to the similar. Further, since the Rationalists, arguing against them, say that craftsmen aim at resourcefulness if at anything else, "but you, having observed one thing upon one thing, will be without resources for treatments, or, being forced to observe many things upon the same thing, you will never practise the art", they reply, "But you have observed", they say, "that we use transition to the similar, from which resourcefulness comes to us." For suppose someone suffering from vertigo bled after a fall, and was then rid of the affection: having observed this, we use phlebotomy on another. First, then, one might ask them how they have apprehended that the vertigo patient was rid of it through the haemorrhage and not through this fall. But one need not yet argue against them before showing in how many ways they use transition to the similar. They say, then, that they use transition to the similar sometimes from remedies to remedies, sometimes from places to places, and sometimes from affections to affections. From remedies to remedies, as when they adopt the medlar instead of the apple for dysentery patients; from places to places, as when we transfer something observed in muscular or sinewy parts, for example from the thigh to the arm; and from affections to affections, as when they use the things observed in haemorrhages for the bite of a haemorrhous (snake). In so many ways, then, they use transition to the similar.

It is right, then, to ask them, first in the case of remedies, how they have used it: whether attending to similarity of power, or to the similarity of the attendant features, as when they adopt the medlar instead of the apple. Do they adopt them thinking that they are alike in astringency, or seeing that both are round, and alike in colour and to the touch? For if they say they make the transition attending to the power, I mean the astringency, they admit that they seek the causes of astringency, by which beneficial things benefit. And together with the power of the beneficial things the power of the harmful things is also apprehended. But they must seek something more too, not only that it is astringent; for many things are astringent but do not do the same thing, as copper scale, while astringent, also cleanses the parts. For if it is known that pepper benefits by heating, it has been apprehended that what is now harmful harms by cooling. But if they say that they choose similar things attending to the similarity of the features, shall we say, "Do you reckon similarity thus, if all the features are similar?" But it is impossible for all the features of any things to be similar, for then they would be the same, and not similar. Clearly, they will say, attending to the similarity of some features. Then we shall say: "You make the transition attending either to more of them, or to an equal number, or to fewer." If to fewer, almost everything would be similar, for all things resemble one another in some respect. If to an equal number or to more, why, we shall say, in cases of haemorrhage, just as you have used leek leaves, have you not likewise used garlic and onion leaves? For these are similar in most respects. And for chilblains, why, as with turnip, not also with radishes? And for stomach patients, why, when wormwood is not available, do they not here use the juice of horehound? For these are almost indistinguishable. And for dropsy patients, why do they not often use turnip instead of radish? And in general one should look for something similar to the observed things but having the opposite power, and ask them whether, because of the similarity, these should be used for the same conditions, the similarity being judged by the senses, as they demand. One could use the same argument for the other cases. For straight away it must be shown to them that they cannot make the transition either from features to features or from affections to affections. For shall we say, "Do you attend to the similarity of the features in respect of power?" But they will not say so, for they do not examine the power, but the similarity of the features as perceived by sense. Is it, then, if they are similar in more of the features, or in an equal number? But inflammation and induration are similar in most respects, yet they require an almost contrary regimen, similar in no respect. And oedema, hernia, scrofula and meliceris preserve much similarity to one another, yet the treatment differs very greatly. Further, those who bring up blood through rupture have almost all their features most similar to those who do so through erosion or the opening of a vessel, yet the same treatment does not suit them all. In this way, then, it can be shown that transition to the similar, as the Empiricists hold it, is impossible.

Next it is consistent to show how the Rationalists can use transition to the similar, which some call not transition to the similar but analogical reasoning. For they say transition to the similar belongs to the Empiricists, and the mode corresponding to transition to the similar they call analogical reasoning, which they say the Rationalists use. We, however, have no quarrel with those who change the names; we shall point out the thing itself, which anyone who wishes may call as he likes. We say, then, that some symptoms accompany the causes, others the affected places, others the powers, and others the patients themselves. The Rationalist distinguishes all these, and knows upon which one must observe and upon which not. Whether the others are present or not, he pays no heed to those that contribute nothing useful to treatment. And when the syndrome seems to vary by one of the useless symptoms, he uses the same [remedies], as though the syndrome were similar. But the Empiricist, since he observes upon the syndrome as a whole and has no power of distinguishing symptoms, must use a different treatment whenever any symptom whatever is lacking or in excess, as though the syndrome were changed, not knowing that with the excess or lack of some symptoms the syndrome really changes, as with inflammation, induration, oedema and hernia, but with others no longer. For in cases of opisthotonus and emprosthotonus the inflammation seems to differ, but since the symptom belongs to the patient, and not to the cause, the place or the power, the treatment does not change. The Empiricist is also ignorant of this, that sometimes the syndrome is similar, yet the same treatment must not be used. For see: the symptoms are equal and similar in those who bring up blood through rupture, the opening of a vessel, and erosion. Let the cough be the same in every case, and the quantity of what is brought up; the rest too the same and similar; and yet a different treatment is adopted. The Rationalist, then, knowing the usefulness and uselessness of the symptoms, will often use the same [remedies] when the syndrome seems dissimilar to most people. For example, some are called opisthotonic, some emprosthotonic, and some tetanic; these seem to have a different syndrome. But the Rationalist knows, say, that the cause is an excess of blood, the affection is of the muscles, and the result is the same; for he will use the same treatment for inflammation. For he attends only to the symptoms mentioned, and dismisses the patient's symptom as useless. For being drawn forward, or backward, or equally, is a symptom of the patient, and watching for it contributes nothing useful to treatment, any more than weeping does. And when the syndrome seems similar, he uses a different treatment in accordance with his understanding of the cause, as with those who bring up blood through erosion or through rupture. For the Rationalist, dividing the symptoms by reference to the things that indicate what is beneficial, and picking out the useful symptoms, and using the remedies able to oppose these symptoms, will often use the same treatment when the syndrome seems different; and again, when it seems similar, he will adopt a different treatment. For treatment consists in what can oppose the causes that bring on the symptoms. The Rationalist, then, apprehends each of the remedies that oppose the disease-producing causes, and is not ignorant of which symptom it is by nature fitted to oppose, because he divides up the syndrome, as we said. But the Empiricist, observing the beneficial things upon the syndrome as a whole, cannot know what is by nature fitted to oppose what. And being ignorant of this, he is not able to use transition to the similar either. For in what respect the beneficial thing benefited, he himself admits he does not know.

"How, then," someone might say, "does the Rationalist distinguish the useful and the useless among the symptoms?" It must be said: by reference to the targets that give indication. For knowing that these symptoms reveal the targets that indicate what is beneficial, while those are not of this kind, he keeps watch on the useful ones and dismisses the others. And from the apprehension of the useful symptoms comes also the ability to use transition to the similar. Sometimes he transfers not the whole treatment but some part of it. For as he divides up the syndromes, so too he divides the treatments. And he knows which of the remedies in the treatment counteract the symptoms brought on by the causes, and which those arising from the places or from the powers. For he knows that this symptom comes from the causes, that one from the places, and that one from the power; and that from the cause the kind of remedies is prescribed, from the place the manner of use, and from the power, to put it for the present, the measure. So when the cause is the same, and the symptoms revealing the cause are apparent, but the place is not the same, nor the power the same, he will adopt the same kind of remedy, but no longer the [same] place and manner. And if the cause is not the same, but the place is the same and the power the same, he will not adopt the same kind of remedy, but the same manner and measure. Since, then, the Rationalist is able to divide both the syndromes and the treatments, he can, guided by the similarities of the syndromes, transfer certain parts of the treatment according to what is fitting. But the Empiricist, who busies himself neither with the cause nor with symptoms revealing causes, or place, or power, will not be able to do this. And for this reason he cannot use transition to the similar either. For he does not know in what respect the syndromes resemble one another. And for this reason he cannot divide up the treatment either, and apply the remedy able to counteract the present symptom. For if he says he is able to do this, I mean to divide the symptoms of the syndromes, and [to divide] the treatment, knowing in what respect each thing benefits and harms, he will admit that he is capable of apprehending hidden causes. And if so, he will admit that he is able to take the remedies from indication too.

Since, then, the things that give the Empiricists' sect its form, observation, history and transition to the similar, are impossible, we have shown that observation is useless without reason and impossible in itself. Useless, since there is need of reason to decide upon which symptoms the treatments should be made; for not even they think one should observe upon all the things that have preceded and are present in the patient. Impossible, because, since these are many, it is not really possible for them all to coincide so that the same syndrome occurs. I mean the same kind and number of symptoms, and magnitude, and order, and right moment, and the like. History, we have shown, is superfluous, because it tests what is recorded by trial; and impossible, because it cannot record in addition either the magnitudes of the symptoms or the right moments, without which apprehension of what benefits cannot come about. And transition to the similar we have discredited by showing that it must of necessity be brought back to the examination of the powers that harm or benefit.

Since, then, we have argued against the Empiricists in summary, next we must speak against the Methodists. Whoever argues against them must grant what is common to the sects and do away with what is distinctive of theirs. The Empiricists, then, arguing against the Methodists, will try to show that it is impossible for the beneficial things to be taken from indication; but we shall grant that it is possible to take the beneficial things from indication. That the indication comes from apparent things, however, we shall not grant them. We shall further grant the Methodists this too: that indication does not come from symptoms, whether one or several. But this we shall not grant: that the symptoms are altogether useless. For it seems to us that the symptoms often reveal the things able to indicate what is beneficial, although for indication the symptoms are altogether useless. The Methodists put forward arguments of this sort. They say that when the symptoms are the same but the affections on which the symptoms rest differ, we do not use the same treatment, as in phrenitis, both that from constriction and that from flux. And again, when the affections are the same but the symptoms differ, we use, they say, the same treatment, as in pleurisy and phrenitis, if both affections are from constriction. Since, then, when the symptoms are the same we use a different regimen, and when they differ we sometimes use the same, for this reason the symptoms are altogether useless for treatment. For when the affections are removed, the symptoms are removed with them, and when they arise, they arise. And for this reason they say the affections are useful, since when these arise the symptoms occur and when they are dissolved the symptoms are dissolved; but the symptoms are useless, having no force over them. And if, they say, the symptoms do give indication, they indicate nothing beneficial, but rather something harmful: as fever [indicates] cooling, or indeed giving drink, or a desire for wine and a bath [indicates] giving wine and taking [the patient] to the bath. Since, then, the symptoms either indicate nothing, or nothing useful but rather something harmful, for this reason, they say, we reject the symptoms, but the affections, as able to indicate what is beneficial, we accept. They also put arguments of this sort to show that the symptoms are not [indicative] of beneficial things: "If the same thing does not indicate contraries, and those in distress from constriction and from flux need contrary things, indication of beneficial things does not come from distress." But one can turn this argument back against them and show that not even an affection gives indication in this way: "If those whose body is constricted by cold and by corruption need different things, and the same thing does not indicate different things, constriction does not point to what is beneficial." The Methodists put the question in another way, thus: "If different things do not indicate the same thing, and those with fever and those with cough sometimes indicate the same thing, indication does not come from fever and cough." We shall turn it back thus: "If those who are racked and those who are relaxed by bile need the same things, and different things do not indicate the same thing, what is beneficial is not pointed to by constriction and flux." Such, then, are the things the Methodists put forward to show that the symptoms are useless.

We shall first show that by what they themselves do they admit that the symptoms are not altogether useless; the use which the symptoms provide we shall point out principally in the exposition of the Rationalist sect. That the Methodists think the symptoms useful for treatment would become clear from the following. They themselves require that those who are delirious in any way be laid in darkness, whether they are delirious through flux or through constriction, for they think light increases the derangement. But lethargic patients, they say, should not be laid in it, whether they are sunk in stupor through constriction or through flux, for they think darkness aids the stupor. How then, we say, if the symptoms indicate nothing, do you lay those delirious through constriction in darkness, when the darkness intensifies the constriction? And again, the lethargic through flux in daylight, when the flux is intensified by it? For in such cases they seem to neglect the affections altogether and attend to the bare symptoms. How then could they be useless, when they plainly have such force that they compel one to neglect the underlying targets, and not only to neglect them, but even to do the opposite of what the targets indicate? For constriction indicates relaxing; but those who shut the delirious up in darkness do not relax but, on the contrary, constrict. And though flux indicates checking, those who bring the lethargic through flux into daylight intensify the flux by the same means. To this they say: "We do not adopt these things because the symptom indicates them, but because the symptom gave a counter-indication to us and does not prevent us adopting what the target shows." For what gives counter-indication, they say, indicates what is beneficial but does not permit us to do what the affection prescribes. To this we say that if counter-indications are useless, then the power too, which often does not allow us to adopt what the target indicates, would be useless. But the power must be examined, since something useful for treatment comes to us from it; and yet the power too gives counter-indication. Just as, then, you think the power useful when it gives counter-indication, so you must admit that the symptoms too are useful. Besides this, they also absurdly adopt darkness for phrenitics. For if darkness intensifies the constriction, and the constriction, when intensified, intensifies the derangement (for the symptoms are intensified and relieved along with the affections), clearly they do the opposite of what they should; for by increasing the affection they also increase the derangement. Such, then, is the argument about the symptoms.

That the affections do not indicate what is beneficial, as the Methodists think, we shall show by the very means by which they themselves tried to prove the symptoms useless: by these same means we shall point out that the affections too do not indicate what is beneficial. For we say that when the affections are the same but the causes differ, we do not use the same treatment. Retention of urine, for instance, is a single affection; but if it arises from a stone, we cut for the stone; if from inflammation, we apply poultices; if from over-distension of the bladder, we use a catheter, or, like Erasistratus, we stand the patient up on his knees, touch the tip of the urethra with *aphronitron* (foam of soda), and so on. Yet if the indications of beneficial things arose from the affections, then when the affection is the same, the same indications of the same beneficial thing would also arise. But they do not arise; [nor] would different affections indicate the same thing. As it is, however, when the cause is the same but the affections differ, we adopt the same treatment. For cholera and jaundice are different affections (they themselves more or less agree that the one is constricted and the other fluxional), yet in both we adopt evacuation. Since, then, when the causes are removed the affections are removed along with them, and when they are established, these are established; and further, when the causes are different, even if the affections are the same, we use a different treatment, while when the causes are the same, even if the affections are different, we use the same treatment: for this reason we examine both the affections and the causes and the affected places. One can also show from the following that, in the same way, the same affection, for instance the constricted, arises from different causes. For fire, when it strikes, condenses the surface, and cold likewise. But although the affection is the same, we use a different treatment because of the difference of the causes. What comes from fire we heal by douches and by poultices able to detach the scabs; what comes from cold by hot fomentations, scrapings of turnip, and similar things. If they say that from both a relaxing and identical regimen is adopted, we shall say that, if the regimen differs in nothing, we shall do no wrong by exchanging them either: we shall foment the one burnt by fire with the same things, and poultice the one harmed by cold, and use on him the drugs that act against scabs. But we do not do this, for they are harmed; therefore it must not be said that the treatment is the same. Further, the same cause produces different affections. From plethora some become inflamed, and inflammation is a constriction; others haemorrhage, and haemorrhages are fluxes; yet the treatment does not change with the difference of the affections. For evacuation is the resolution in both, contrary to the [cause, not the] affection. For the indications ought to arise not from the things that produce but from the things produced, as they themselves also agree. The Methodists accept these [affections] as causes, since they produce the symptoms; but they say they do not indicate insofar as they are causes, but insofar as they are koinotētes (communities). Nothing prevents the same thing, they say, from being both a cause and a koinotēs and other things too. For as the apple is tasted, seen and touched, but when we say it is sweet we do not call it sweet insofar as it falls under touch, so nothing prevents the affections from being the effects of some things and also productive of others. But when we say, they say, that they indicate, we say that they indicate neither as effects nor as productive of something, but as koinotētes. Just as the Methodists, then, say the symptoms indicate nothing beneficial because the same ones arise from different things and different ones from the same, so we too, since we see the same affections arising from different causes and different ones from the same, say that they are useless for the indication of beneficial things. For one [affection] does not always indicate the same thing; [otherwise], in retention of urine, clearly, we would always use the same treatment. Just as they themselves say that redness does not indicate, thinking it is of the kind of an effect, so we too shall say that the affections are useless for indication, being sometimes causes and sometimes effects. And yet one might say to them: how does redness not indicate its own alteration? For a koinotēs too is seen through it, since it is seen in many different cases; and a koinotēs is sameness in many things.
