If, then, it both indicates and is common to many, why do you not make your indications from this and from such symptoms, which are clearly apparent, rather than from the affections, constriction and flux, which are in no way apparent? And it is not demonstrated what the affection is; it is most absurd to say that an affection is imperceptible. Now if flux and constriction alone were koinotētes, there would be some plausibility in saying that they alone indicate. But since the symptoms too are common to many, why does indication of beneficial things not arise from the symptoms as well? They reply: "But because they are not koinotētes proximate and necessary for those who treat, for this reason we reject the symptoms. For when the affections are the same but the symptoms differ, we use the same treatment; and when the affections differ, we use a different regimen, as has been shown somewhere." For these very reasons, we shall say, we too, seeing that the same thing happens with the affections which you observed in the symptoms, now reject them as useless. For it is possible, as a surplus, to establish this too, that apprehension of the affections is useless. For apprehension of the cause, recognition of the troubled place, and the measure of the power suffice for treatment; whether it is constriction or flux, I say it is superfluous to apprehend. But this argument will be stated later, when we go through what use the apprehension of the affections provides.

This must be said to the Methodists: that the affections do not indicate what is to be done, but their own removal or elimination, which is what anyone would pray for. This is plain even to laymen and to irrational animals, that affections indicate elimination and health preservation. But craftsmen do not need this indication; they want to know the things by which the elimination of the affections and the preservation of health will come about. They need, then, the things that indicate the particular beneficial things, by which one may attain health and preserve it. It is in this that craftsmen differ from laymen, if they apprehend the things that indicate the particular beneficial things. But if the indication of beneficial things came from the affections, those who have them would themselves know by what means health must be secured. But this they do not know; what the affection indicates, they do know. For since it indicates removal, they send for the doctors who are able to remove the affections.

One can also recognise from the remedies applied that it is not the affections but the causes that indicate the treatment. For the remedies are opposed not to the things that arise but to the things that produce them: as evacuation is contrary to plethora, but to no affection, such as inflammation or fever. When the plethora is removed by the evacuation, the affection that arose from the plethora is removed along with it. But not because it is removed along with what produces the affection was the remedy opposed to the affection. One can also know, from comparing the symptoms that follow from plethora and from evacuation, to what the remedy is opposed: plethora weighs down by its excess, while evacuation, by reducing the excess, removes the heaviness; again, plethora distends the vessels, while evacuation brings them to collapse. And you would find the other remedies opposed to the causes, but none to the affection. Further, one might learn from this too: if constriction is no remedy, nor flux either, but rather indicates some affection, and flux is contrary to constriction, then constriction indicates not evacuation but flux. Likewise flux will indicate constriction. So what we adopt is the same as what the affection indicates [only if it is an affection]. But harmful causes indicate their contrary, and what these indicate we adopt. Therefore it is not the affections but the causes that indicate what is beneficial. That the symptoms, then, are not wholly useless, and that the affections cannot indicate what is beneficial, while the causes do indicate it, has been sufficiently shown.

Next we must examine whether the koinotētes which the Methodists posit are apparent or not, and whether indications can arise from the koinotētes or not. They define medicine, in accordance with their own opinion, as knowledge of apparent koinotētes, but they say that "apparent" does not mean apprehensible through sense perception. For no condition is apprehended through sense perception; rather, they call "apparent" what is apprehensible from itself, even if it does not fall under the senses. For what they call "apparent" is roughly the evident. Now someone arguing against them ought to point this out too, that they do not know how to use Greek words. But so that we may not seem to be quibbling over a word, we shall grant them "apparent" in the sense in which they use it, and shall show that the koinotētes are not apprehensible from themselves. And first we shall show that Thessalus, the founder of their sect, set out signs of the koinotētes, as [conditions] that evidently are not of a nature to be apprehended from themselves. For in the patient, he says, constriction can be apprehended from the bodies being hard to evaporate through. Likewise he also sets out certain marks of flux. But perhaps they will say: "You are arguing against a man, and not against our sect." Leaving Thessalus aside, then, we shall demonstrate the proposition. First, then, we shall use a common argument concerning the two conditions, showing that they are not apparent and are not apprehensible from themselves; then we shall also show separately that each of the conditions is not apprehended from itself. Now they themselves agree that not every condensation of the body, nor every retention of a secretion, is constriction. For country people are in a state of compactness, yet they are not in constriction. And the retention of what is proper is not constriction: when a woman's purgation is held back because of pregnancy, it is a retention of a customary secretion, but it is not constriction. Further, not every rarefaction of bodies and secretion is flux. For children, women, and men who live delicately are by nature rarefied, and the secretion of residues is a kind of secretion, not flux. Nor will they say that those who reach a crisis through the bowel, or through urine, sweats, or haemorrhages, are in flux; for in that case they would have had to resist the excretion. Since, then, not every condensation and retention is constriction, nor every rarefaction or excretion flux, it is clear that for one who attends to the bare symptoms themselves it is impossible to apprehend flux or constriction, and they must be judged from other things. For just as the other symptoms, whether they are natural or unnatural, are apprehended not from themselves but from other things, so too are constriction and flux. What is meant will become clear from the following. Natural symptoms bear a great resemblance to unnatural ones; for the same things are natural for some and unnatural for others. For example, the unnatural black colour is like the natural one: for us it is unnatural, but for the Indians natural. And unnatural postures resemble natural ones; for some people are by nature more loose-jointed than others. And a sharp nose and hollow eyes are deadly symptoms for some, but for others these same things are natural. And movement and immobility, if they occur by choice, are natural, but if involuntarily, unnatural. From these things it is quite clear that those who attend only to the symptoms themselves cannot recognise the natural and the unnatural; but in some cases one must examine the cause that brings [the symptom] on, as with movement, whether it is by choice or involuntary; and also with colour. For since colour comes from the humours, and the blood shows through in the colour, one must consider whether the blood is in its natural state. You will see this from its use: if the blood provides all its other use unhindered, and neither distends nor weighs down, you will say that the colour is natural. Whether a posture is natural you will apprehend from the use of the limb, as in dislocations. And in some cases whether it is natural is apprehended from the place in which it occurs. So too condensation and rarefaction are natural for some and unnatural for others. The condensation of old people is natural for them, but unnatural for children; and the rarefaction of children, in turn, is natural for them, but unnatural for old people. And some are condensed by their way of life, like country people, and others by circumstances, and yet they are in a natural state. For this reason it is not possible to apprehend the conditions by looking at bare condensation of bodies and at flux; one must also refer these to something else and so judge whether they are natural or affections. For they say: "We distinguish natural symptoms from unnatural ones by due proportion and disproportion. For when the body has condensation and rarefaction in due proportion, the animal is healthy; but when one of them is intensified and exceeds due proportion, it must be ill." We must say to them, then, that the proportionate and the disproportionate is something other than the conditions. And if the affections are judged by disproportion, it is admitted that they are not apprehensible from themselves. Then [argue] thus: the proportionate and the disproportionate is not apparent, but is apprehended from the results; for if it benefits, it is proportionate, and if it harms, disproportionate. How then, when this proportionate and disproportionate is not apparent, could the things apprehended from it be apparent? And if the proportionate and disproportionate were judged in relation to the power, not even so would the disproportionate be plain; for the power is not apparent. And since the disproportionate is not apparent, clearly the koinotētes are not apparent either; for these too are certain disproportions. Further, we must say to them that none of the natural things appears [as] unnatural, but things appear as natural or unnatural. For pain and other things of that sort appear unnatural. But doctors want to apprehend not what sort of things are unnatural, but whether they are. For a sharp nose and hollow eyes are apparent to all people; but whether they are natural or unnatural, to doctors alone. For in this doctors differ from laymen, that in what is apparent they are able to apprehend something hidden, which laymen are not able to apprehend. Then, [if] the unnatural is not apparent, and the koinotētes are unnatural, clearly they are not apparent. It is worth considering this too: whether any person ever sent for one of the doctors on the grounds that he was distressed by a disproportionate condensation or rarefaction. And if no one has ever come to perceive the koinotētes, how is it reasonable to say that they are apparent? And if the koinotētes are not apparent, how do they suppose the art to be knowledge of apparent koinotētes?

Now we shall speak separately about each of the conditions, and first we must speak about constriction. They say, then, that constriction is condensation and retention of things that need excretion. Now the things retained must be either beneficial, or harmful, or neither. If they are beneficial, it is unreasonable to excrete them. If neither, clearly it is not an affection either. It remains, then, to say that it is constriction when the things retained do harm. But what harms is a cause. So the constricted state is apprehended from a prior apprehension of the causes. For in order to know that [a body] is constricted, one must know beforehand that the things retained are harmful. And with the apprehension of the harmful things comes, at the same time, the recognition of the causes; or rather, the recognition of the harmful things is the apprehension of the causes. And again, the harmful things themselves, which are causes, are not apprehended from themselves. So not only is constriction not apparent, but neither are the things from which constriction is apprehended.

Flux they define as disproportionate rarefaction of bodies, and secretion of things that need to be retained. Now that disproportionate rarefaction is not apprehended from itself has been shown. But the things secreted, whether they ought to be retained or not, from what do they apprehend this? For these are not of a nature to be apprehended from themselves; so clearly flux could not be apprehended directly either. For in order to recognise flux, one must first apprehend what is proper; and what is proper must be judged from its use; and the use from many results, and since these are not apprehended from themselves, flux is not recognised [from itself]. How then is it reasonable to say that it is apparent? And roughly what the Rationalists say is most difficult to apprehend, this the Methodists say is apparent. For what they call flux differs in nothing but name from what the ancients named colliquation. And the ancients thought colliquation and excretion so hard to distinguish that Erasistratus openly admits the very great difficulty of the judgement. He speaks thus: "It is very hard to distinguish excretion from colliquation." And Hippocrates refers the judgement to ease and distress, saying: "If they are purged of what ought to be purged, it is beneficial and they bear it easily." So when two ancient men, competing for first place, both agree that excretion is hard to distinguish from colliquation, and the one sets out not even a sign of excretion but only points out the difficulty of the matter, while the other refers the judgement to a criterion hard to apprehend, the Methodists think this is apparent. Further, in those who are being dispersed through the imperceptible [pores], from what will they say they apprehend flux? They cannot do so from collapse, because collapse occurs not only when bodies are emptied by flux, but also with constriction when the menses are retained. And swelling likewise occurs not only with constriction, when things needing secretion are retained, but also with flux, when the fluids are poured out and distend the bodies. That perceptible collapse and flux are not the same will be clear from this: if collapse is perceptible, and swelling is contrary to collapse, and one thing is contrary to one thing, [then] not swelling but constriction will be contrary to flux. And if they say that swelling is the same as constriction, we must show them the contrariety of the definitions. For they say that constriction is a compression and binding of the bodies. Constriction, then, is binding and compression of the bodies; but swelling is a pouring out and distension of the bodies. And bodies are distended either through plethora or through pouring out. It is evident, then, that constriction and swelling are not the same. But if they agree that collapse is something other than flux, and swelling something other than constriction, they are saying that the koinotētes are not apprehended from these, and they admit that the conditions are apprehended from other things and not from themselves, if indeed they apprehend them from collapse and swelling, which are other than the conditions.

Some say that in those who are dispersing [their substance] imperceptibly, they apprehend the flux from the fact that the bodies are soft, crumbly and enfeebled. Against them we must say: then if the bodies are hard and stretched tight, they will not call it flux, yet they must admit it. So if some patients are of the kind Hippocrates describes, brought by extreme want to the point of having the skin hard and stretched tight, along with the other things found in those who are dispersing, shall we use the regimen for those who are dispersing? One must admit [that we shall]. How then is flux apprehended from looseness? For even when tension and hardness are present, it is flux none the less.

Next, that even if the koinotētes are apparent, they indicate nothing beneficial, one could show by this, saying that it is a different thing for the common features themselves to indicate, and for the things able to indicate to be apprehended from the common features. Now the Methodists say that the common features themselves indicate; but we say that the apprehension of the common features is useful for the recognition of the particulars that are able to indicate. And the theorems, being in a way common, point to the apprehension of the particulars. For in 'spontaneous fatigues announce diseases' we apprehend the relation of the particular spontaneous fatigue to plethora; for here 'diseases' must be taken as plethora. So the knowledge of the universal supplies the apprehension of the particular that is able to indicate the beneficial.

But one must not think that we suppose the things indicative of the beneficial to be apprehended directly through the theorems. For the theorems do not reveal the hidden things which we need for treatment as indicating, but they disclose the relation of the hidden things to the apparent ones. We may understand the use of the theorems more carefully in this way, by fixing our argument on 'spontaneous fatigues announce diseases' itself. That a spontaneous fatigue is evident, even laymen know. But that plethora is revealed through the spontaneous fatigue, laymen do not know, for it is hidden; but practitioners know it, having apprehended from the theorem the relation of the spontaneous [fatigue] to plethora. For he who framed the theorem, setting out from the relation of the spontaneous fatigue itself to plethora, and apprehending that the spontaneous fatigue is an effect of plethora, framed it. For since he knew a certain twofold most general division of causes, and that of the causes some are outside us and some in the bodies themselves, he thought it necessary that, when nothing external is troubling [us], we would not be distressed otherwise than if the cause is present in the bodies. And since of the things in the body those that weigh it down weigh it down by an excess of substance, so that if it is in due proportion it neither weighs down nor troubles, he put these together into one reasoning and made this theorem: 'spontaneous fatigues announce plethora'. For the use of the theorem must be shown from the same reasonings from which the framer of the theorem set out when he framed it. This universal, then, shows that wherever there is spontaneous fatigue, there is certainly plethora. Yet he did not apprehend the plethora from the theorem, but the relation of the fatigue to the plethora, and from the relation, the plethora. In a way, then, he apprehended the plethora through the fatigue; but the theorem was the cause of his apprehending it through that. And examining the other theorems we shall find the same use. This, then, is how we hold universal and, as it were, common apprehension to be useful.

But the Methodists think that the koinotētes themselves indicate the beneficial things. For they say that the constricted affection indicates that one must loosen, and that the fluxional calls for the astringent regimen; and they suppose that the remaining koinotētes indicate evident beneficial things, about which we shall speak. That the koinotētes do not indicate, we shall establish by the following. The things on whose elimination the sick become healthy are the things of which remedies are eliminative. And the things of which remedies are primarily eliminative are those from which the indication of the beneficial things arises. But remedies are primarily eliminative of the particular causes, and if indeed of diseases, then of the particular causes; and so, if anything, the diseases would indicate the beneficial, and the koinotētes do not indicate the beneficial by being koinotētes. And if the remedies applied are eliminative of the things that indicated, the koinotētes are eliminated by the particular remedies. But if the koinotēs were eliminated, those who at that time were sick with the same koinotēs would have become healthy, although nothing had been eliminated by it [in them]. And if what indicates is what is eliminated, and the koinotētes indicate, clearly the koinotētes will be eliminated. To this the Methodists say: 'We call the koinotēs the same and one, not because it is a single body continuous with itself, if it is observed in several cases, but inasmuch as it is the same form.' For just as humanity too is said to be a koinotēs, not as one unified body then observed in all human beings, but as a certain likeness in several, so too, they say, we must understand the koinotēs. So just as, they say, when one human being is destroyed, the humanity which we see in all is not destroyed with him, but only the humanity of that one individual, so too when a particular koinotēs is eliminated, the koinotēs found in all is not eliminated, but only the particular one. We must say to them, then, that if the koinotētes, in so far as they are koinotētes, indicate the beneficial, humanity too, being a koinotēs, would indicate the beneficial. But humanity indicates nothing; so neither would any other koinotēs be indicative of the beneficial. Further, if the koinotēs is a sameness in several things, and the koinotētes, in so far as they are koinotētes, indicated, then distress and redness too, observed in several affections, would indicate something beneficial; but they indicate nothing; so neither do the remaining koinotētes have an indicative nature. We must also ask them this: are the koinotētes affections or not? If affections, how is it that no one has ever perceived them? People perceive fever, inflammation, heaviness and distension, and send for doctors because of these; but no one has ever perceived constriction or fluxion. Nor, by Zeus, did anyone ever send to a doctor as being troubled by disproportionate constriction or rarefaction. But if they are not affections, how do they say that the indications arise from the affections, when constriction and fluxion are not affections? And this too must be said: if the koinotētes had an indicative nature, then above all the koinotēs of the koinotētes would indicate. For there is a certain likeness between constriction and flux, in so far as both are koinotētes. But this indicates nothing; so neither do the rest. They say there are not only two koinotētes but more, some in regimen and others in surgery: in regimen, the constricted, the fluxional, and the mixed, [and] magnitude; and that there are four times of diseases: beginning, increase, peak and decline; and the acute and the chronic, and the paroxysm and the remission. In surgery, what is foreign by nature, by place, by time, and several others. But we need not now go into detail about the targets in surgery; for the targets in regimen that have been set out will suffice for the present purpose.

They brought in the koinotētes mentioned because they had no way of proceeding in practice. For since it followed for him to use any astringent whatever in every flux and any loosening agent whatever in every constriction, but they did not find anything indicative of the difference between remedies, they brought in the koinotētes mentioned as well, so that a different treatment might be found according to their difference. So they say that these koinotētes indicate the difference of the remedies; for the treatment is found to vary according to the combination of some of these.

We shall show that none of the things mentioned can be indicative of remedies. And first, that the magnitude of the koinotētes does not indicate the magnitude of remedies one may learn from this. In treatment we need not simply a magnitude of remedies (for all remedies come with some quantity of magnitude), but this particular magnitude. But the magnitude of the koinotētes will not indicate the magnitude of this particular remedy, but simply magnitude. Yet, as I said, one must apply not simply a magnitude of remedies but a magnitude of such and such a size. For if we apply simply magnitude, since all remedies are conceived with some quantity of magnitude, we shall apply all remedies and make no distinction, which is most unreasonable. But if, when the magnitude of the koinotētes indicates simply a magnitude of remedy, they themselves apply this particular magnitude, they will not be applying what the target indicates. For the target indicates magnitude in common, but they apply this particular magnitude. Perhaps they will say: 'We apply it not because the magnitude is particular, but because it is a koinotēs; and the same thing happens to be both common and particular.' To this we shall say that if the koinotēs indicates, then what it indicates must not be left undistinguished in the particular case, since magnitude accompanies every remedy. And this same argument can be transferred to the koinotētes as well.

Next we shall show that the times of diseases do not indicate what is beneficial either. Before this argument, a few things must be gone through about the difference between times. Doctors speak of two kinds of times: those of diseases and those of remedies. From this the treatment too would become quite clear. They say that the times [of diseases] are the movements of the causes. There are four kinds of movement: beginning, increase, peak and decline, and these are also the names of the times. The times of remedies, they say, are the periods suitable for applying them. Suitable periods are those in which the things that demand the application of the remedy are present, and none of the things that prevent it exists.

Most people think that the times of remedies and of diseases do not differ in reality, but only in conception. For they say that the time of the remedy and the time of the disease arise at the same period, since the time of the remedy is found while the disease is at some time. And it is possible, they say, for the same thing to be spoken of differently when it is referred to one thing and to another. Just as the way up and the way down, being one and the same road, is sometimes called the way up and sometimes the way down according to the relation of those going up and those going down, so it is with the times too. For the time of the disease and the time of the remedy are one and the same. One speaks of the time of the disease when referring it to the movement of the cause, and in another way of the time of the remedy when referring it to the fitness of the moment for applying the remedies. And they say it happens that both times arise together, and that it is impossible to take a time of remedy without a time of disease.

Against them it must be said that if the times of remedies and of diseases are the same and do not differ in reality, then in every time of disease there would have to be a time of remedy too. But we do not apply remedies in every time of disease; for, he says, 'When diseases are beginning, if anything seems right to stir, stir it; when they are at their peak, it is better to keep quiet.' So the times of diseases and of remedies are not the same. Often, too, we apply remedies, such as purging or phlebotomy, when there is no disease, but one is suspected to be coming. So, for example, surgeons, with patients about to be operated on for hernia, apply phlebotomy when they see that they are overfull. And Hippocrates too advises that extreme good condition be reduced without delay, and the reduction comes about through remedies. If, then, when diseases are at their peak there are no times of remedies, and when there are no diseases there are times of remedies, it is evident that they differ not only in conception but also in reality. Further, within one time of a disease one takes several times of remedies. In the decline of a disease, say, an enema is applied, and an anointing, and a poultice, and food; and each of these has its own time. And sometimes we select the same remedy in several times of diseases: phlebotomy is applied both at the beginning of diseases and in the increase. From these things, then, it is apparent that there is a difference between the times in reality. In addition to what has been said, one must also recognise this: diseases have four times, beginning, increase, peak and decline; but these are not times of remedies. For neither beginning nor increase nor peak nor decline is a time of a remedy. Further, the times of diseases, both the general and the particular, can be written down; but of the times of remedies the general can be written down, while the particular no longer can, for some such reason as this. The times of diseases, both general and particular, are judged by one and the same criterion, and the criterion can be written down. But the times of remedies neither have the same criterion, nor is it possible to write down the criteria of the particular times. How this is so we shall now show. The times of diseases are judged by the quality of the movement of the cause; and beginning, ascent, peak and decline, which we call the times of diseases, are names of the quality of the movement of the cause. If a movement that was not there before begins to arise in us, and causes distress as it arises, we call such a movement the beginning of the disease; if the movement advances towards greater, the increase; if the increase comes to a standstill, we name it the peak; and if the movements diminish, we call it the decline. Since, then, the names of the times are the same both for whole diseases and for particular paroxysms, and the criteria are the same (for they come from the quality of the movement of the cause), it is clear that both kinds of times can be written down. For we say that each thing, such as the causes, the affected places and the like, can be written down when the targets from which the particulars are grasped can be written down. That the intervals of diseases are not the times, and that the times are not taken from intervals, either for whole diseases or for particular ones, is clear from the fact that the intervals are not the same in all cases while the same things are called times. That the times of whole diseases and of particular paroxysms differ is clear from the fact that within one time of the whole disease several times of particular paroxysms arise. For at the beginning of the onset of a disease a particular paroxysm both begins and increases and peaks and declines; and when the whole disease is already at its peak, a particular paroxysm makes its beginning. How, then, both kinds of times of diseases can be written down has been stated. How both kinds of times of remedies cannot be written down, we shall now show.

The times of remedies are not taken from the movement and substance of the cause; for then the same thing would always be applied, such as phlebotomy at every beginning of a disease. And he who said, 'When diseases are beginning, if anything seems right to stir, stir it; when they are at their peak, keep quiet', does not select the remedies starting from the time. For he knew that at the beginnings of diseases the power has not been brought down, and for this reason does not stand in the way of applying the remedies, whereas at the peak of the disease, being already worn out, it does not bear the disturbance caused by the remedies. So Hippocrates selects the application of remedies starting not from the time but from the power. Nor indeed is the time of the remedy found from the interval of the times in diseases, as some think. For since the intervals differ greatly, it is impossible to say what interval one could name as prescribing [it]. The times of general remedies, then, are taken from the presence of the things demanding the remedies (these are the causes) and from the absence of what could prevent them (this is weakness of the powers). But the times of particular remedies are taken not only from these but also from other things, which cannot be written down. For remedies are applied above all in the abatements, since then what demands them is present and the power holds up; but the interval of the abatement is not the same in all cases. Suppose the interval of the abatement is six hours. Which of these hours, then, shall we fix as the time of the particular remedy, when not all patients are in the same condition? Suppose the circumstances demand phlebotomy and the power does not oppose it, so that, as far as this goes, phlebotomy should be applied. But one patient must also be given food right after the phlebotomy, because he cannot bear fasting; for another it is beneficial to fast; others need sleep before the phlebotomy; others something else; and it is impossible to write all of this down. In such great variety, then, it is impossible to say what part of an hour one could prescribe as a time fitting every remedy, or what target one could write down from which the particular time could be taken; for different things befall different people. Since, then, the intervals of the abatements in which we apply the remedies are not equal in all abatements, and the circumstances are unlike, and the symptoms differ, and with each of these the particular time of the remedy also changes, it is clear that it is impossible to write down any target from which it could be taken. But the attending physician, starting from what is present and demands the remedies, from the absence of what could hinder them, and from reasoning about the remedies that ought to be applied after this, will form a conjecture of the particular times of the remedy, lest perhaps the targets do not differ in reality. Since, then, the targets from which the general times of remedies are taken can be written down, while those from which the particular times are grasped cannot, they reasonably say for this reason that the times of general remedies can be written down but those of particular remedies no longer. This having become evident, the difference between the times in diseases and the times in remedies would be clear in this respect too. For if they did not differ in reality, then both kinds of times of remedies could be written down just like the times of diseases. But since the targets from which the times are taken differ greatly, it is reasonable that the times too differ from one another. For just as the targets of the times in diseases differ in reality from the targets of the times in remedies, so it is plausible that the times themselves differ in reality. These, then, are the things one needed to know beforehand about the times.

The Methodists believed that the times give indications for some such reason as this. They saw that not all times are suitable for taking food or a remedy, but that at some times these are taken with benefit and at others with harm, and they believed that this happens according to the difference of the times. From this, then, they supposed that the times of remedies are also targets for food. Hippocrates also misled Thessalus when he said: 'When the disease is at its peak, then it is necessary to use the thinnest diet as well.' For [Thessalus] supposed that he had taken the quality of the food by starting from the time, not understanding the manner of the man's approach. For he did not examine such an administration by making the time his target; rather, he took the measures of the power from the time, and the quality of the food from the power. He made this clear by what he adds, for he said that one must 'judge together whether the patient will hold out.' For the times often prevent us from applying what is demanded by the power, but a time never shows what is to be done.

Since, then, what demands something is the target of what is demanded, while what prevents us from applying what is demanded would not be a target, for this reason the time too, which sometimes prevents us from applying what is demanded, would not be a target. For if anyone sets down everything that prevents as a target, he will be forced to say that the power is a target of evacuation, and so too the patient's timidity, and a father, and a master. For these often prevent us from applying evacuation when there is plethora: the power not bearing the removal, the sick man not permitting it out of timidity, a father forbidding it, and a brother or a master. Just as no one with sense would call these targets, so neither shall we say that the times are targets because they will often prevent us from using remedies or administrations. 'Then,' someone will say, 'Hippocrates speaks wrongly: "At the beginning of diseases, if anything seems to need stirring, stir it; but when they are at their peak, it is better to keep quiet."' Not wrongly, we shall say. For he does not make the beginning his target when he thinks fit to apply remedies at the beginning of diseases; rather, from the beginning he notes that the measures of the power have not yet been diminished, and infers that it can bear the removal. The peak, on the other hand, points to weakness of the power. For at the peaks the causes are strong and the power weak; for this reason he thinks fit to keep quiet. For it will seem reasonable to carry out the elimination of the causes at the peaks of diseases, when the causes are most powerful. And if it were wholly harmless to apply the remedy, this would have been done. But it is not so. For the remedies, first, because they are all contrary to nature, necessarily also distress the power when applied. Second, since they distress what is proper [to the body], [and what is proper] is entangled with the disease-producing causes, in the eliminations of the causes there comes about a diminution of what is proper no less than of what is foreign.

But first one must not be ignorant of the nature of the remedies and the service they provide. For the remedies by themselves are not such as to bring about the removal of the causes, but need nature to work with them; and they give nature almost only the starting point and the beginning, while nature completes the rest by herself. When she is strong, she both endures the harmfulness of the remedies, bears the elimination of what is proper easily, and is able to expel what distresses her. But when she is oppressed, which happens most of all at the peaks, she is harmed more by the remedies applied, becomes weaker from the elimination of what is proper, gives way more to the causes, and is in no way able to expel what makes [the body] sick. And when nature, having strained herself, is unable to expel what distresses her, she is greatly exhausted by the very straining. For these reasons, then, Hippocrates thinks fit at the beginnings of diseases to stir, if anything needs stirring, but at the peaks to keep quiet.

Perhaps, then, someone will think from this that the power points to what is beneficial. But one may learn from the following that the power indicates no remedy. If the power, when it is sufficient, indicates some remedy, then in healthy people, because it is sufficient, it will indicate the remedy. But in healthy people it indicates no remedy. Therefore neither in the sick will a moderate [power] indicate anything beneficial. Since, then, in those cases where the power will give an indication, what demands [a remedy] is not present, we do not apply a remedy; and it is clear that the power indicates nothing beneficial. For the target must indicate what is present. [It is clear] that the power can, as I said, prevent us from applying what is demanded, but is not a target of a remedy.

The relation that the power has to remedies, the times have to administrations [of food]; and the relation that the demanding causes have to remedies, the power has to administrations. That it is the power and not the time that demands a small administration is shown by the intensification; hence to those recovering from illness we give a little food, which is what the power demands. But if the intensification indicated small food, one ought to let these people eat their fill. For when the target that points to small food is not present, the one who applies what is not demanded is ridiculous. But they say that the beginning indicates the need to restrict. Then it is clear that in all cases we shall apply restriction at the beginnings, and in those who have *alphoi* and *leukai* [white skin diseases] up to the intensification. And if the beginning stretches out over a long time, clearly the one using such a regimen will waste away. But perhaps they will say to us: 'For what reason do you at the beginning, say, not give food at the beginnings to those with pneumonia and those suffering acutely like them, although at the beginnings the power is adequate?' Because, we shall say, the time prevents us from giving food although the power demands it. So [the time] does not indicate restriction; rather, since it does not let us apply what the power demands, no one would reasonably set it down as indicative of the contrary. Likewise the other times too prevent or permit the use of what is demanded, since the power has been changed in them more or less. Yet this does not indicate anything beneficial. And when they say that the peak demands little food and the decline more varied food, one must ask them how they will use their targets if there are two patients, one with pneumonia and in the decline, the other with ophthalmia, whose disease is still at its peak: will they dare to give the pneumonia patient more and more varied food than the one troubled by ophthalmia? But they would not dare to give the more varied food. And if this is clear, [it is clear] that the variety and the small amount of food are not taken from the times but from the measures of the power.

One might also be puzzled at this: how they think that the time of the disease indicates sometimes the quantity and sometimes the quality of food, as the Methodists maintain, and sometimes indicates the difference of the remedies, and sometimes demands the difference of the remedies. For when they say that the increase demands little food, the beginning more generous food, and the decline more varied food, they are saying that the times of diseases indicate both the quality and the quantity of the food. But when they say that the beginning indicates preventing growth, the increase restricting and relaxing without elaboration, the peak leading towards the more soothing, and the decline assisting the resolution, they will be admitting that the times demand a difference of remedies. How, then, is it not absurd to say that the same thing, having acquired no difference, indicates different things? To this they will perhaps say that according to the Rationalists too the same thing indicates different things. For bile lying [in the body], since it harms, indicates its own elimination. One must reply to them that bile indicates only its own removal, but there are several ways of removal: we either eliminate it or temper it. Then, we shall say, bile appears to be indicative of different things in different respects: in so far as it weighs [the body] down, of elimination; in so far as it bites, of tempering. But how the times, having no such difference, could demand different things, it is impossible to say.

That a time does not indicate quality or quantity of food can be learned from this: what indicates the genus must also indicate the quantity. For without a difference each of the indicating things indicates the genus of what is demanded; but having acquired a difference, it will indicate what differs within the same genus. Since, then, the power indicates the genus of administration, accordingly it will also indicate the quantity and the quality. For without a difference it indicates the genus of administration; but having acquired a difference, it will also indicate what differs within the genus. Hippocrates too evidently makes the power the target of the quantity of food, where he says: 'Growing things have the most innate heat; they therefore need the most food; otherwise the body is consumed.' And it is clear that he takes the quality from the difference in power. For he says somewhere: 'Grain unaltered for the young at their very prime, but for the old altered to the end.' From these things, then, it is evident that the power without a difference demands the genus of administration, and with a difference the quality. But a time indicates neither quality nor quantity of food. Further, if the times of diseases indicate the quality and the quantity of food, they will indicate this either for their own persistence or for their removal. For what indicates shows either its own preservation or its removal. If, then, the times give the indication of the quantity and quality of food with a view to what persists, how is it not ridiculous to say that we give food of a certain quantity and quality in order to preserve the times of the diseases? But if the times give the indication for their own removal, the quantity and quality of food must appear to have some contrariety to the times. For only contraries are capable of removing contraries. But neither the quantity nor the quality of food is contrary to the times, neither to the beginning, nor the increase, nor the peak, nor the decline. For the same cause is not contrary to several things; for one thing is by nature contrary to one only. By the same argument we shall show that the times of diseases do not indicate the difference of remedies either. For if the times give the indication neither for their persistence nor for their removal, since one thing could not be contrary to several, and there is no other mode of indication, it is clear that the times indicate nothing beneficial. Moreover, anyone who looks at the nature of contraries will know that it is not even a contrary. For contraries are things in the same genus standing farthest apart from one another. But time and food or quantity are not ranked under the same genus. That neither the quality nor the quantity nor the differences of remedies can be taken from the times has been sufficiently demonstrated by us.

Now we shall show that the beginning does not indicate what prevents growth, which the Methodists think it indicates. For since many diseases reach their peak together with the beginning, such as apoplexy and the acute diseases, what would anyone say the beginning indicates in such diseases? It will not indicate preventing growth, for he will say that the disease has reached its peak together with the beginning; [so he must say] either that the beginning indicates nothing in such diseases, or something else, and not preventing growth. Now to say that it indicates nothing, when one has recognised it as a target, is most ridiculous. And if it indicates something else, and not what they themselves think, then they were wrong to say that the beginning demands preventing growth.

This error arose for them from another false assumption. Thinking that every disease passes through the four [times], and laying this down for themselves as true, they supposed that it must follow that the beginning of diseases demands the prevention of the increase. So this too has escaped them: not every disease begins, increases, reaches its peak and declines. The acute diseases, such as apoplexy, reach their peak with the onset. And diseases that come to a crisis cut off one time, the decline. For crises resolve diseases around the peak, while they are still increasing towards the greater; and it is possible through remedies to resolve the disease at the beginning and to cut short the remaining times of diseases. If, then, it is possible at the beginning both to evacuate the disease and to resolve it through remedies, why ever do they hold that the beginning indicates preventing growth, and not rather the reduction or the removal [of the disease]? And if they say that it is not the beginning but the condition that indicates the reduction and removal of diseases, why then, we shall say to them, do you apply not what the condition indicates but what the beginning indicates? For through what is demanded by the condition, what is indicated by the beginning also comes about: whoever reduces or removes the disease also prevents its increase from occurring. But perhaps they will say that the commonality of the beginning, being more immediate, compels us to apply what it indicates, since it prescribes immediately what is to be done; whereas the condition, while demanding that diseases be removed, does not indicate the means by which this must be done. But the means by which one must prevent [growth] in the particular case, of which [the beginning] indicates preventing growth, that is, the 'by which means', is taken from other things; and in the same way the condition too indicates only the removal of diseases, while the means by which this must be done must, it seems, be taken from something else. Therefore it is better to use as a target not [only] the beginning but the condition as well. Then this too must be said to them: it appears, on our view, that every beginning is a kind of mixture. For two commonalities come together into the same thing, the beginning and the condition, and each of the commonalities indicates something different, but the beginning seems to you to be the more immediate and more necessary commonality, because you attend to it. It is clear from this, then, that all affections are mixtures of commonalities. For every condition occurs at some time. So not only the time is a commonality, but also the condition. You do wrong, then, in thinking that the mixed [condition] is one particular kind of affection, and not saying that all affections are mixtures.

Further, this doctrine of the Methodists is also foolish: that one must always use constricting [remedies] at the beginnings of diseases. The doctrine took its cause from this: many inflammations are settled at the beginning by constricting and repelling [remedies]. But every inflammation, according to them, is a constriction. So it appeared absurd that constricted things should be settled by condensing [remedies]. And when we say that the restoration of the apparent [symptoms] comes about through the repelling of the offending [matters], being quite unable to see this they say that one must treat the beginning by constricting [remedies]. 'For we do not repel the causes,' [they say], 'but [act] so as to render the bodies resistant to affection. For the contraction and binding of the bodies,' they say, 'making the bodies more resistant to affection, prevents diseases from taking hold. For the increase is prevented,' they say, 'not only by reduction of diseases, but also by the resistance of the bodies to affection.' One must reply to them that it is impossible to make bodies resistant to affection by increasing what harms them; and besides, one ought to secure resistance to affection for bodies before they fall ill. For it is so that disease may not arise that we need resistance to affection; but once the bodies are affected, one must bring about the removal of what is disposing them [to disease]. And since the constricted condition is a condensation of the bodies and a difficulty in their transpiring, and constricting [remedies] condense the surface and make it hard to transpire, it is clear that constricting [remedies] will assist the increase of what is constricted rather than oppose it. And the magnitude the affection would have reached in its own times comes about at the beginning through the remedies. They also appear to apply the opposite of what is demanded by the beginning. For the beginning indicates what prevents growth, but the quality of what is applied seems to assist the increase. One of two things [follows]: either one must not attend to the beginning, as indicating wrongly, or the quality of what is applied is not applied to good effect.

That constricting [remedies] are applied with benefit at the beginnings of inflammations everyone would agree; but it is worth asking them the cause of what happens. For to say that resistance to affection arises from constricting [remedies] is ridiculous, as we have shown. Let them learn from us that the constricting remedies reduce and resolve diseases by repelling the offending [matters] and transferring them to other, unaffected places. This too must further be said to show that the beginning does not indicate remedies that prevent their growth. These things [are] according to them: if the beginnings of diseases [indicate] constricting [remedies], they either possess some quality or not. Now to say that the beginnings of diseases are without quality is ridiculous; for they would not come to perception if they had no quality. So either the quality of the beginnings is different alongside each of the conditions, or the quality of each beginning is not different from the condition to which it belongs. If, then, the quality of the beginnings is different, this appears as another commonality of the affection, which they have passed over; but if the quality of each beginning is the same as that of the condition to which it belongs, why shall we not, at the beginning of diseases, use the relaxing treatment against constriction and the constricting treatment against flux? For it is unreasonable for us to take a different stance towards the beginning, as though it did not possess the same quality as the condition of which it is the beginning.

That it is ridiculous to think that resistance to affection arises in bodies from the constricting treatment, by which bodies are condensed and constricted, one could learn from this. If condensation, contraction and hardness of bodies were a cause of resistance to affection, those with inflammation and induration, and those whose skin is hard and stretched tight from extreme want, would be more resistant to affection than the healthy. For the healthy have softer and looser bodies, and all the more so the healthier they are. Further, if resistance to affection were judged by hardness, old men, who have harder bodies than children, ought to be thought more resistant to affection. For if they have by nature that resistance to affection which the Methodists say they secure by art, how would it not be reasonable for them to be more resistant than the young?

But the Methodists do not know how one must judge a human being's resistance to affection, and therefore they will not be able to secure it either. For one must not judge the resistance to affection of human beings by hardness and softness, as with stone, iron, wood and the like, but by the bodies' being able to perform their own functions unimpeded. So whoever wishes to secure resistance to affection must not consider how the body will become hard, but how the powers of the parts will be increased and the parts will perform their own functions unimpeded.
